hints: Look at P first. It contains both $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ joined together. Recall which linkage joins carboxylic acids to amines.
Look at Q. It is $\text{C=O}$ with carbon groups on both sides and no $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$. Decide if this is an aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid or ester.
Look at R. It is $\text{C-OH}$. Count how many other carbon atoms are directly attached to that same carbon to decide between primary, secondary and tertiary.
walkthrough:
Recognise P as an amide link**
See the group $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH-}$. A carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ directly bonded to nitrogen is the amide functional group, $\text{-CONH-}$. It is formed from a carboxylic acid and an amine, so call it an amide, not an amine.

Recognise Q as a ketone**
See the group $\text{-COCH}_{3}$ attached to the benzene ring. The carbonyl carbon is joined to two carbon groups, the ring on one side and $\text{CH}_{3}$ on the other. That pattern $\text{R-CO-R'}$ is a ketone.

Classify R as a secondary alcohol**
See the group $\text{-CH(OH)-}$. The $\text{OH}$ bearing carbon is attached to two other carbons, one $\text{CH}_{2}\text{O-}$ group and one $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH-}$ group, plus one H. An alcohol on a carbon attached to two other carbons is a secondary alcohol.

Final answer: P: amide
Q: ketone
R: secondary alcohol

hints: Check each carbon for four different attached groups. Focus on carbons with $\text{OH}$, $\text{NH}$ or branching, as $\text{CH}_{2}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups cannot be chiral.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
A chiral carbon has four different atoms or groups attached and no plane of symmetry. Work along the chain. $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups have two H atoms so they cannot be chiral. The isopropyl $\text{CH}$ has two identical $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups so it cannot be chiral.

Spot the only chiral centre**
The carbon in $\text{-CH(OH)-}$ is bonded to: $\text{OH}$, H, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{O-}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH-}$. All four are different, so this is the single chiral carbon atom. Circle it.
Final answer: Circle the $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbon in the side chain $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_{2}\text{-NH-}$.

hints: Warm dilute $\text{HCl}$ breaks amides by hydrolysis. Find the $\text{CO-NH}$ linkage in acebutolol and mark the bond between C and N.
walkthrough:
Recall which bond acids hydrolyse**
Warming with dilute hydrochloric acid hydrolyses amides. Water adds across the $\text{CO-NH}$ bond to give a carboxylic acid and an amine (as its ammonium salt in acid). Esters also hydrolyse, but there is no ester here, only ether, ketone, alcohol and amine which do not split. So the break must be the $\text{C-N}$ bond of the amide P.
Final answer: Draw a line through the amide $\text{C-N}$ bond in P, between $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{NH}$.

hints: After breaking the amide $\text{C-N}$ bond, the acyl side $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO-}$ gains $\text{OH}$ to become a carboxylic acid. Count its carbons to confirm it is the smaller fragment.
walkthrough:
Build the acid fragment**
The left hand fragment from P is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C=O}$. On hydrolysis the $\text{C-N}$ breaks and $\text{OH}$ from water joins the carbonyl carbon to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$. This four carbon acid is much smaller than the rest of the drug molecule, so it is the smaller molecule.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$, butanoic acid.

hints: Scan acebutolol for the groups each reagent detects: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ for alkaline iodine, basic $\text{-NH-}$ for indicator, any $\text{C=O}$ aldehyde or ketone for 2,4-DNPH, and aldehyde only for Tollens.
Recall the positive observations: yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_{3}$ for iodoform, blue or purple alkaline colour for indicator, yellow or orange precipitate for 2,4-DNPH.
Remember that ketones give a positive result with 2,4-DNPH and iodoform reagent but do not react with Tollens reagent, which oxidises aldehydes only.
walkthrough:
Use alkaline iodine to find the methyl ketone**
Acebutolol contains $\text{Ar-COCH}_{3}$, a methyl ketone. This gives a positive iodoform reaction. Warming with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$ in $\text{NaOH}$ gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_{3}$.

Use indicator to find the basic amine**
Acebutolol contains a secondary amine $\text{-NH-}$. Amines are basic and accept $\text{H}^{+}$. Universal indicator in a basic solution turns blue to purple. The phenolic ether, amide, ketone and alcohol do not affect this strongly.

Distinguish carbonyl tests**
Both aldehydes and ketones react with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine to give a yellow or orange precipitate of the hydrazone. Acebutolol has a ketone, so a yellow or orange precipitate forms. Tollens reagent, ammoniacal $\text{Ag}^{+}$, oxidises aldehydes to give a silver mirror but ketones cannot be oxidised further, so with this ketone there is no reaction. Write none.

Final answer: alkaline iodine solution: yellow precipitate formed
universal indicator solution: blue / purple (alkaline) colour
2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine: yellow / orange precipitate formed
Tollens reagent: no reaction, none

hints: Carboxylic acids are very resistant to reduction. Recall which powerful hydride donor reduces acids all the way to primary alcohols, since $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is too weak.
walkthrough:
Choose the strong enough hydride**
Butanoic acid to an alcohol is reduction of $\text{-COOH}$ to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ reduces aldehydes and ketones only. You need the stronger reducing agent lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$, in dry ether, followed by acid work up.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$, lithium aluminium hydride.

hints: Reduction of butanoic acid gives a four carbon alcohol of formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. Draw its isomers and look for the one with a carbon attached to four different groups.
walkthrough:
Find the chiral butanol**
Compound N has formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ as an alcohol. Butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, has no chiral centre. Butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, has the C-2 attached to H, $\text{OH}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, four different groups, so it exists as a pair of optical isomers. Draw it in skeletal form with a four carbon zigzag and OH on carbon 2.
Final answer: Skeletal formula of butan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$.

hints: An alcohol that still reacts with Na to give $\text{H}_{2}$ but is not oxidised by acidified dichromate must have no H on the $\text{C-OH}$ carbon. Decide which class of alcohol this is.
walkthrough:
Identify a tertiary alcohol**
All alcohols react with sodium to give hydrogen and an alkoxide: $$2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_{2}$$ Only primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised by acidified $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the $\text{OH}$ so it cannot be oxidised. The tertiary isomer of formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{3}\text{COH}$.
